content: The combination therapy of glecaprevir and pibrentasvir has been shown to be both safe and effective for individuals with chronic kidney disease and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, covering all six major HCV genotypes. However, this regimen is not approved for use in individuals with decompensated liver disease. In 2018, access to this treatment in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) was limited. As an interim solution, where genotype-appropriate, previously recommended combinations from the 2016 WHO HCV treatment guidelines may be considered for individuals with advanced chronic kidney disease (grades 4 and 5). Individuals with tuberculosis (TB) and HCV co-infection are at increased risk of both infections. Clinical evaluation for HCV treatment should include screening for active TB using a four-symptom algorithm (cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats). If none of these symptoms are present, active TB can be reasonably excluded; otherwise, further investigations are required. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) used for HCV treatment interact with liver metabolic pathways, which can alter drug levels when co-administered with rifamycins (e.g., rifampin, rifabutin, rifapentine). Therefore, concurrent treatment of HCV and TB should be avoided. Active TB poses a higher immediate risk due to its potential for secondary transmission and life-threatening complications, so TB is typically treated before addressing HCV. In individuals with HCV undergoing TB treatment, the risk of hepatotoxicity is higher than in those with TB alone, though severe hepatotoxicity is rare. Monitoring liver function tests can help detect hepatotoxicity early. Managing co-infection with HCV, TB, and multidrug-resistant TB is particularly challenging due to drug-drug interactions (DDIs) between DAAs and second-line antimicrobials. Limited data exist on managing individuals co-infected with HCV, HIV, and TB, and specialist referral may be necessary to address additive side effects, pill burden, and DDIs. For individuals who fail DAA therapy, retreatment options are limited. While DAAs achieve sustained virologic response (SVR) rates exceeding 90% across all HCV genotypes, an estimated 2–5 million individuals globally may not achieve SVR and will require effective retreatment. A highly effective initial treatment regimen is critical to avoid retreatment dilemmas. Evaluating adherence and potential DDIs can guide decisions for those who fail DAA therapy. Currently, a single pangenotypic regimen is approved for retreatment: the fixed-dose combination (FDC) of sofosbuvir, velpatasvir, and voxilaprevir. Clinical trials involving over 300 individuals, including 46% with cirrhosis, demonstrated high efficacy of this triple DAA regimen for those who failed prior DAA-containing regimens, with SVR rates ranging from 93% to 99%. The lowest SVR rate was observed in individuals with genotype 3 infection and cirrhosis. However, this regimen is contraindicated in individuals with Child-Pugh Class B or C cirrhosis or renal failure. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir has also been approved for retreatment in patients who failed sofosbuvir-containing regimens or those who failed treatment with either a protease inhibitor or an NS5A inhibitor (but not both). In the absence of these regimens, extending the initial DAA therapy to 16 or 24 weeks while reinforcing adherence may be an alternative retreatment option. In 2016, the WHO estimated that only 13% of individuals diagnosed with HCV infection had initiated treatment. To address this gap, eight key good practice approaches to service delivery have been identified to support the implementation of clinical recommendations for universal treatment and the use of pangenotypic regimens. These include comprehensive national planning for HCV elimination, simplified and standardized care algorithms, strategies to strengthen linkage from testing to care, integration of hepatitis services with other health services, decentralized testing and treatment, community engagement and peer support, efficient procurement and supply management, and robust data systems to monitor care quality and coverage. National planning for HCV elimination should be based on local epidemiological context, existing healthcare infrastructure, and available resources. Simplified algorithms for testing, treatment, and monitoring can be adapted for national use. Strategies to strengthen linkage to care should address barriers such as stigma, discrimination, high costs, and transportation challenges. Integrated service delivery systems can facilitate access to hepatitis testing and treatment, particularly in high-risk populations such as people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), and incarcerated individuals. Decentralized services, including task-sharing and differentiated care strategies, can improve access to care, especially in LMICs. Community engagement and peer support can reduce stigma and discrimination, promote service access, and support adherence to treatment. Efforts to increase the availability of DAAs and diagnostics at the country level include selecting appropriate products, determining the availability of generic medicines, registering DAAs with national regulatory authorities, forecasting demand, and implementing efficient procurement mechanisms. Data systems are essential for monitoring the quality and cascade of care, including diagnosis, treatment initiation, and cure rates. Specific populations, such as PWID, face unique challenges in accessing HCV care due to criminalization, discrimination, and stigma. High-coverage harm reduction programs, including needle and syringe distribution and opioid substitution therapy (OST), are effective in preventing HCV transmission and reinfection. Routine targeted testing for HCV, HBV, and HIV is recommended for PWID, with regular follow-up testing for those at ongoing risk. Linkage to care and treatment should be facilitated through targeted interventions, including testing and treatment in drug dependency services or prisons.
